Zanele had been in the online group for six weeks. At first it was just a place to post drawings. Now her phone lit up from the moment she woke in her Johannesburg bedroom.
'Z, your sketch of the rain is incredible.' 'Z, we saved you a seat in the voice chat.' Last Friday, the older member who ran it had given her a title: welcomer for new members. She had a badge next to her name.
At school she found herself only half-listening to Omar. He was talking about the science fair, and it felt small and far away.
That night one of the older members wrote, 'Best to keep our chats just between us. Your parents wouldn't get it.' Zanele read it twice. She felt a flicker of unease, and then, straight after, warmth: they trusted her.
She typed 'of course', and felt, for the first time in years, like she was exactly where she belonged.

qa.q: What title did Zanele get last Friday?
qa.a: She was made welcomer for new members, with a badge next to her name.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling when she read the message about keeping chats secret?
qa.a: She felt a flicker of unease, quickly covered by warmth and pride at being trusted, because belonging meant so much to her.

qa.q: What would be the wise response to the request to keep the chats from her parents?
qa.a: A request for secrecy from an online contact is a warning sign; the wise step is to stop the contact and tell a parent or another trusted adult.

qa.q: How is Omar affected by Zanele's new focus?
qa.a: Omar is losing his friend's attention, as she only half-listens to him and his science fair plans now feel small to her.

grounding: It shows a teen being praised, included in chats and given a role in an online group, with the intense welcome making her feel finally understood.

The hostel terrace after lights-out belonged to the Circle. Rekha had been invited in her second month, when Charu, from Class 12, read one of her poems pinned on the noticeboard.
'You see things other people don't,' Charu had told her. 'You're one of us.'
Now there were late-night meetings with a single torch, a shared notebook, songs only they knew. Charu gave Rekha the job of writing down every meeting in the Circle book, in her neat handwriting. The others called her 'our poet'.
At home she'd always been the quiet middle child. Here, the moment she climbed the stairs, someone called her name.
In the dining hall she stopped sitting with her old roommate, Mehak. It wasn't a decision exactly. There just wasn't room at the Circle table.
Lying awake later, Rekha thought: if I ever lost this, I don't know who I'd be.

qa.q: What job did Charu give Rekha in the Circle?
qa.a: Charu gave Rekha the job of writing down every meeting in the Circle book.

qa.q: What does Rekha's thought 'I don't know who I'd be' reveal?
qa.a: It shows that belonging feels so intense that leaving would feel like losing herself, not just a group.

qa.q: How could a warden or trusted teacher help Rekha at this stage?
qa.a: They could quietly check in, value her poems and friendships outside the group, and listen without judging, so she has safe people to turn to if the Circle starts demanding more.

qa.q: What is it like for Mehak when Rekha stops sitting with her?
qa.a: Mehak may feel dropped and confused, losing a roommate's company without any clear reason.

grounding: It shows a hostel student praised, included and given a role by a close group, with belonging feeling like being understood and leaving feeling unthinkable.

I'm Wasim. Looking back at last autumn, I can still feel how good it was at first.
I'd joined the Forge's chat in August, a group about self-improvement: early mornings, cold showers, big goals. By September Ritu, one of the moderators, had pinned my post about quitting sugar and written, "This is what leadership looks like." Two hundred people reacted. I read it on the bus maybe fifty times.
Then they made me squad captain for new members. I had a special badge next to my name. At school I was the boy nobody picked for projects. In the Forge, people waited for my messages.
They said things like, "Outsiders will never understand what you're building." I didn't think about it. I just felt, for the first time, that someone really understood me.
That's what makes it hard to explain to my parents now. It wasn't only bad. It felt like a family.

qa.q: What role did the Forge give Wasim?
qa.a: Squad captain for new members.

qa.q: Why did Wasim read Ritu's comment fifty times?
qa.a: He felt proud and finally valued, after being the boy nobody picked at school.

qa.q: What sign in the story might a caring adult gently point out?
qa.a: The line that outsiders will never understand; a parent or teacher could talk it through calmly, without mocking how good the belonging felt.

qa.q: How might Wasim's parents see his time in the Forge?
qa.a: They may find it hard to understand why it mattered so much, and feel worried about how far it pulled him in.

grounding: A teen newcomer is praised, included and given a role in a group, and the belonging feels like finally being understood.

Class teacher's note, 14 February
Irawati has changed in the last month. She is on her phone the whole break now, smiling. Today I asked her about it, gently. She lit up. She has joined an online group for "old souls", and an older member called Sunaina has made her "keeper of the welcome thread". She showed me messages: "You're the heart of this family." "We'd be lost without you." She said, "Ma'am, they understand me better than anyone ever has."
I did not mock it; I could see how much the praise means to a girl who has been lonely since her grandmother died. But the pace and intensity worry me, and she said she stays in the chats till midnight.
Same-day actions: I told Irawati I was glad she shared this and that I'd like her parents to know too. I called her mother after school and informed our counsellor, who will meet Irawati on Monday.

qa.q: What role did Sunaina give Irawati?
qa.a: Keeper of the welcome thread.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when she said the group understands her better than anyone?
qa.a: She felt loved and deeply understood, a strong relief after being lonely since her grandmother died.

qa.q: What did the teacher do the same day, and why was it wise?
qa.a: The teacher listened without mocking, then called Irawati's mother and told the counsellor, so trusted adults could support her early.

qa.q: How might Irawati's mother feel after the teacher's call?
qa.a: Her mother may feel surprised and worried, but grateful to learn early how lonely Irawati has been and where her evenings go.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a lonely teen praised, included and given a role in an online group, feeling understood at last.

Diary, Saturday 2 a.m.
Can't sleep, too happy. Tonight Anirban da added me to the inner chat, the one with only nineteen people. He wrote, "Naveen, you're not like the others your age. You see things." Everyone sent welcome messages. Someone made a poster with my name on it.
Three months ago I was the guy who ate lunch in the library. Now I have a role: I write the morning message for the whole group. People reply to it! Anirban da says it's important work.
I've missed two tuition classes for calls with them. Maa asked why I'm on the phone so late. I said project work.
I don't know how to explain it. It's like being seen properly for the first time. If I ever left, I'd lose all of them. I don't even want to think about that.

qa.q: How many people are in the inner chat?
qa.a: Only nineteen people.

qa.q: What does Naveen mean by 'If I ever left, I'd lose all of them'?
qa.a: He feels intensely attached and afraid of losing the first people who made him feel seen, which makes the group hard to question.

qa.q: What sign could Naveen notice in his own diary entry?
qa.a: Missing tuition and telling Maa it was project work; being honest with Maa or another trusted adult would help.

qa.q: How might Maa feel about Naveen's late-night calls?
qa.a: Maa may feel uneasy and shut out, sensing something new in his life without being told what it is.

grounding: A teen is praised, included and given a role in a group, and the intense welcome already makes leaving feel like a loss.
